+### The three coordination papers, read 2026-08-16
+
+Assigned in [`06-track-b-channel.md`](06-track-b-channel.md) task 4. **What each assumes about cooperation is the column that matters**, and all three make it explicit — which is a change from the general state of this literature.
+
+**ATM — AI-Atomic-Framework** (Huang, Eagl · [arXiv:2607.00041](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00041), 29 Jun 2026). *Read: abstract, §1, §2 (partial), §3.1–3.2, §3.7, §4.7, §5 intro–5.1. **Not read end to end** — treat as `[V-abs]`+ and re-read §5–6 before relying on the benchmark numbers.*
+**Claims** a specification-grounded pre-write admission layer: agents form write intents, a Content Identifier broker routes each to parallel admission / deterministic composition / serialization / fail-closed refinement, and — the load-bearing part — *"Governed shared writes are ultimately applied by a neutral steward rather than directly by the proposing agents."* §3.2: *"an agent does not directly hold final write authority over the shared filesystem."*
+**Measured:** a 12-scenario deterministic fixture matrix, three archived runner cases, ATM-AdmissionBench v0.2 over 20 scenarios / 42 mode-level comparisons, three archived same-file boundary cases, a three-week external-adopter study, and a recovery-routing benchmark. **The paper is unusually careful about what this is not:** §4.7 *"the paper does not yet report a controlled comparative benchmark, confidence intervals, or power analyses"*, and §5 states head-to-head comparison against CodeCRDT, CoAgent, S-Bus and others *"remains future work."*
+**Assumes about cooperation:** everything, stated as four assumptions (§3.2) — *"there is a single authority governance domain… governed shared writes are applied through the neutral steward rather than bypassing the brokered path… adapter declarations… over-approximating rather than understating potential conflicts… validators are available."* §3.7 disclaims cross-machine, cross-clone and cross-PR coordination outright.
+**Verdict: ADJACENT, and the most useful negative result we have for W4.** ATM achieves real enforcement — and buys it with a neutral steward inside one governance domain, which is exactly the chokepoint-plus-standing trade W4 predicts. It is the existence proof that enforcement is available *if you have an owner*, and it declines the cross-owner case explicitly. Its assumption 3 is also a warning: enforcement holds only while nobody bypasses the brokered path, which in a cross-owner world is a request, not a guarantee.
+
+**CoAgent — MTPO** (Lyu, Zhang, Wu, Wei, Chen · Shanghai Jiao Tong University · [arXiv:2606.15376](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15376), 13 Jun 2026). *Read: abstract, §1, §2, §5.1–5.2, §7.2–7.3. Not read end to end.*
+**Claims** classical concurrency control fits LLM agents badly — transactions span minutes of inference, read sets are broad and opaque, and live state can be neither forked nor buffered, so 2PL blocks and OCC discards minutes of work per conflict. Its move: *"the LLM inside each agent can judge whether a conflicting write invalidates its plan, and can repair exactly the operations that depended on it. **Control therefore turns advisory: the runtime informs, the agent repairs.**"*
+**Measured:** ten contended workloads. MTPO within 5% of serial correctness at 1.4× speedup and 1.15× token cost; 2PL deadlocks 0.81×/trial and recovers almost nothing (1.04×); OCC aborts 0.95×/trial, runs *slower* than serial (0.93×) at 1.83× tokens; uncoordinated execution is fast and passes **13%** of trials. Separately, on a bash-only target it grew a 25-tool library online and lifted pass rate 45/71 → 63/71.
+**Assumes about cooperation:** formalised as A1–A3 (§5.1). **A2 (well-formedness):** *"every action on shared state goes through a registered tool, inside its declared footprint, and a delivered notification is consumed before the agent's next action. The agent thus follows the protocol."* **A3 (self-healing):** the notified agent correctly judges what its plan depended on — **measured to fail 5% of the time** (5 of 100 trials, DeepSeek v4 flash). Plus the *"latent object schema assumption"*: footprints enter by declaration, not inference.
+**Verdict: PARTIAL, and the second independent arrival at *advisory*.** Two papers, different problems, both conclude the runtime informs and the agent decides. That makes W4's answer less like one author's caveat and more like the shape of the problem — but note both reach it by design choice, and neither tested an agent that declines to heal. **The number to steal is 13%**: uncoordinated agents passed 13% of contended trials, which is the best evidence in this file that the coordination problem is real at the action level and not just at merge time. Also note A2 is our adversary #4 stated as a premise, and A3's 5% is an *honest* error rate with no adversary at all — a floor under anything we design.
+
+**CodeCRDT** (Pugachev · [arXiv:2510.18893](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18893), 18 Oct 2025) `[V-full]`
+**Claims** agents can coordinate by observing shared CRDT state instead of message passing, with a TODO-claim protocol (optimistic write-verify on a Yjs `Y.Map` LWW register, 50 ms sync wait) carrying a proved at-most-one-winner safety property.
+**Measured:** 600 trials, 6 TypeScript/React tasks × 50 runs × 2 modes, Claude Sonnet 4.5, ≤5 agents. Raw response time from **−21.1% to +39.4%** vs sequential; normalized per 1000 characters, parallel is faster on 5/6 tasks (11–52%) because it generates 82–189% more code. **100% convergence, zero character-level merge failures.** Quality: performance score +25% (d=1.51), code quality −7.7% (d=−0.71), accessibility −5.6%. Scored by an LLM with no human baseline; 13.8% of response-time points removed as outliers.
+**Assumes about cooperation:** total, and structurally — all agents share one Yjs document through one Hocuspocus relay, and the claim protocol's safety theorem holds because agents run the protocol. Stale claims are reclaimed on a 120 s timeout, which handles crashes, not defection.
+**Verdict: PARTIAL for coordination — and direct evidence for W5.** `[V-full]` Manual inspection of a 10% sample (60/600 runs) found a **5–10% semantic conflict rate** (duplicate declarations, type mismatches, broken references), *with 100% character-level convergence*, and task variance from 20% (simple) to 80% (complex). §4.3: *"CRDTs cannot detect semantic inconsistencies."* Our repo asserted this as `[S]`; it now has a measured number attached, with the caveats that it is preliminary, a 10% sample, manually judged, and on six UI tasks under 100 LOC. **This is the cleanest demonstration that convergence and correctness are different properties**, and it is the paper to cite whenever someone answers our problem statement with "just use CRDTs."
+
+**Reading for Track B:** this layer is more crowded than it looks, and `grite` in particular is a serious, measured, git-native prototype of the core idea. Track B's opening is not "a coordination log" — that exists — but *cross-owner, cross-vendor, no shared trust*, which every system above assumes away. **After reading all four: every one of them states its cooperation assumption explicitly, and every one of them assumes a single governance domain.** That is not four independent confirmations that cross-owner coordination is hard; it is four teams choosing the tractable problem. The gap is still open, and it is still open for the same reason.
